title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build 10 sample reports on publicly permitted PJM and ERCOT campuses using permit files and disclosure data, and retain an air attorney to co-sign the methodology. Days 5-25: interview 15 people, namely data center debt originators, private credit underwriters, ABS/CMBS rating analysts, lender counsel and independent engineers, to find who owns power diligence in credit committee and which live deals are closing in the next 90 days. Days 20-30: offer three free reports on live deals in exchange for a 30-minute review and permission to cite, then price the fourth at $25k. Get one independent-engineer white-label LOI. The riskiest assumption is that a lender will make this a closing condition. Test it by asking for the condition in writing.
lineage: mutation of I0836 ('Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Voltus, CPower and ERock are sellers of megawatts, so they have no incentive to tell a lender a campus is uncovered, and none serves the capital-markets buyer. Trinity works for the operator, which is a conflict in a lender report, and it sells hourly permit projects rather than a standardized, comparable score. Independent engineers are the likely adjacent entrants. We sell to them white-label and win on speed, a permit-structured dataset and a lawyer-reviewed methodology. No competitor found in the parent's research sells to lenders, insurers or rating analysts.

competitors.name: Voltus
competitors.what_they_do: C&I demand-response / virtual power plant aggregator. Its 'Bring Your Own Capacity' product sells hyperscalers accredited PJM capacity. Its Google agreement (announced 2026-06-02) aggregates up to 100 MW of accredited distributed capacity in PJM over three years. The Google and Sunrun press releases describe batteries, thermostats and residential solar-plus-storage. Neither mentions backup generators or air permits. This is the most direct competitor for the same buyer need (a hyperscaler needing PJM MW fast), but with a different resource type.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Site says 8.5 GW of DERs, 22,000+ sites and $500M+ paid to customers. It acquired Brightfield AI (2026-06-10). Funding was not disclosed on the pages I fetched.

competitors.name: CPower
competitors.what_they_do: Large C&I virtual power plant and demand-response provider that lists data centers as an industry it serves. It is the incumbent PJM curtailment service provider type that would enroll generator-backed DR. The pages I fetched did not confirm backup-generator enrollment, air-permit handling or MW figures. That CPower historically enrolls C&I backup gensets is my background knowledge, not verified this session.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not verified from fetched content. Established, private-equity-backed incumbent (from memory).

competitors.name: Enchanted Rock (ERock)
competitors.what_they_do: Builds natural-gas gensets and microgrids, and sells 'flexible capacity' and bridge-to-grid power to AI and hyperscale data centers. Its pitch is that customers support their own load first and act as grid assets during shortfalls. It attacks the same 'behind-the-fence MW' problem with new low-emission gas hardware rather than by unlocking existing diesel. It competes for the same buyer budget.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Site claims a 1.1 GW installed base and 99.999% combined reliability. Funding was not disclosed on the pages I fetched.

competitors.name: Trinity Consultants (data center and power team)
competitors.what_they_do: Air-permitting and emissions consultancy with a dedicated data center and power team. It advertises air permitting strategy, emissions testing, engine emissions certification and help with 'air and noise regulatory complexities' for onsite prime power. It could sell permit-modification work per project. It is not packaged as permit-to-dispatch or tied to capacity revenue.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large established private consultancy. Scale not verified from fetched content.

I0836.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for fast PJM MW is verified. Demand for paying to unlock backup diesel specifically is not.

Verified this session:
(a) PJM's 2028/29 auction, 2026-07-14, cleared 138,318 MW at the FERC-approved price cap and was 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement. Demand response was 5% of cleared UCAP. PJM said it will file a Reliability Backstop Procurement and 'Connect and Manage' framework at FERC. It also began facilitating 10+ year bilateral contracts between large loads and supply, including demand-side resources, via an RFP from June 9. https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/2026-releases/20260714-pjm-capacity-auction-procures-138318-mw-of-generation-resources.pdf
(b) PJM Board plan of 2026-01-16: large loads can bring their own new generation or accept earlier curtailment, plus a backstop procurement. https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/2026-releases/20260116-pjm-board-outlines-plans-to-integrate-large-loads-reliably.pdf
(c) Hyperscalers are paying for BYO capacity. Google signed a Voltus deal for up to 100 MW of accredited distributed capacity in PJM (2026-06-02). https://www.voltus.co/press/voltus-google-bring-your-own-capacity-pjm and https://www.voltus.co/press/sunrun-voltus-energy-capacity-hyperscaler-agreements
(d) Texas SB 6 (2025) requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose on-site backup generation. ERCOT may direct them to deploy it or curtail in an emergency. The bill expressly does not authorize violating emissions limits. That is a regulation-forced spend on exactly this permit question. https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm
(e) Pennsylvania's governor and PUC are pushing BYO-generation and curtailment rules for data centers; a PUC-commissioned study warns of PJM reliability failure by 2030. https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjms-reliability-could-start-failing-by-2030-if-data-center-growth-continu/830405/
(f) The rule constraint is real: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/63.6640

Not verified: the 55 GW national and 27 GW Virginia backup-generator figures, the $325/MW-day and $555/MW-day cap numbers, and any RFP, forum complaint or customer purchase specifically for backup-diesel permit unlocking. I found none this session.
I0836.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with 'all idle diesel becomes capacity'. Three changes:

1. Sell interconnection speed, not capacity revenue. Package a 'PJM connect-and-manage / BYOG readiness dossier' for data center developers. It bundles a permit-modification strategy, an emissions-compliance pathway, telemetry and M&V into evidence PJM and utilities can accept for faster large-load interconnection. Charge fixed fees plus a success fee on energization date. Capacity-revenue share becomes a secondary upside.

2. Start where the math already closes. Target fleets that are already Tier 4 or SCR-equipped, or in attainment areas with headroom in existing minor-source or synthetic-minor permits. There the only change is a run-hour cap and emergency-versus-non-emergency classification, with no retrofit. Use the 30-site public-permit headroom map to find these sites. Sell the map itself as a subscription to aggregators (Voltus, CPower), utilities and hyperscaler energy teams.

3. Partner rather than compete. Be the white-label 'permit-cleared MW' layer for Voltus, CPower and ERock, who already have PJM enrollment and hyperscaler relationships but no permit playbook. Get paid per permit-cleared, accredited MW.

Texas is a possible beachhead for the first proof point, because SB 6 forces large loads to disclose and deploy backup generation and has an emissions carve-out. It is not a PJM market, so treat it as validation of demand for the permit work, not as the target market.

Before spending money, do a legal feasibility check: get an air-permitting attorney's opinion on whether emergency engines can be reclassified for capacity participation in VA, OH and IL at acceptable retrofit cost. If they cannot, the idea fails on regulation, not competition."
